proposals.before: Liu Bei continued, I reckoned Sun Quan's worry lay north and that he would need me as an ally, so I went without hesitation.
proposals.after: I reckoned Sun Quan’s worry lay north and that he would need me as an ally, so I went without hesitation.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic English breaks out of Liu Bei’s quoted speech with a narrative tag mid-sentence (“Liu Bei continued, I reckoned…”), which is ungrammatical and obscures that the line is still Bei’s voice.

proposals.before: 〈Jiang Ji’s Treatise on Myriad Affairs notes that Xu Shao’s praises and censures were skewed—he boosted Fan Zizhao and played down Xu Shao the younger.
proposals.after: 〈Jiang Ji’s Treatise on Myriad Affairs notes that Xu Shao’s praises and censures were skewed—he boosted Fan Zizhao and played down Xu Wenxiu.
proposals.reason: The Chinese names the second man 許文休 (Xu Wenxiu), not another Xu Shao; rendering him as “Xu Shao the younger” invents a shared personal name and confuses two distinct people.

proposals.before: He usually wore a plain scholar’s headcloth to meet the Administrator of Fufeng, who said: “Though Duke Ai was unworthy, he still served Confucius as minister; Liuxia Hui would not leave his parents’ state—I wish to press you to take office as Clerk of Merit—what say you?”
proposals.after: He usually wore a plain scholar’s headcloth to meet the Administrator of Fufeng, who said: “Though Duke Ai was unworthy, he still had Confucius as his minister; Liuxia Hui would not leave his parents’ state—I wish to press you to take office as Clerk of Merit—what say you?”
proposals.reason: 猶臣仲尼 means Duke Ai retained Confucius as minister, not that Duke Ai served Confucius; the literal reverses the relationship.

proposals.before: 〈The Records of Huayang Country states that Du came from Guanghan and held the post of provincial attendant.〉
proposals.after: 〈The Huayang guo zhi states that Du came from Guanghan and held the post of provincial attendant.〉
proposals.reason: 華陽國志 is the chronicle title Huayang guo zhi; rendering 國志 as ‘Country’ invents an English book title that obscures the work’s name.

proposals.before: Liang replied: “When the sovereign was at Gong’an he feared Cao Cao’s strength to the north, Sun Quan’s pressure to the east, and Sun Lady brewing trouble at his elbow;
proposals.after: Liang replied: “When the sovereign was at Gong’an he feared Cao Cao’s strength to the north, Sun Quan’s pressure to the east, and Lady Sun brewing trouble at his elbow;
proposals.reason: Chinese 孫夫人 is Lady Sun; “Sun Lady” reverses English name order and obscures the referent.

proposals.before: Cao Cao’s barb is wounded vanity, not acute analysis.
proposals.after: That the Martial Emperor of Wei thought him coached—was that so inferior a judgment?
proposals.reason: Chinese 魏武以為人所教，亦豈劣哉！ asks whether regarding Liu Bei as advised is inferior; it does not assert Cao Cao spoke from wounded vanity.

proposals.before: Pei dismisses Cao’s remark as spite, not truth.〉
proposals.after: This is bitter leftover talk from shame, not measured speech that fits the facts.〉
proposals.reason: The Chinese continuation does not rename Pei or Cao; the idiomatic invents named agents and overstates “spite, not truth.”

proposals.before: His son Miao inherited a Marquis Within the Passes and rose to Colonel of the Chariots and prefect of Hanyang.
proposals.after: His son Miao was granted rank as Marquis Within the Passes and rose to Colonel of the Chariots and prefect of Hanyang.
proposals.reason: 賜 means grant/bestow, not inherit; the son received 關內侯, not Fa Zheng’s posthumous Marquis Yi title.

proposals.before: Zhuge Liang and Fa Zheng differed in temperament yet respected each other’s office.
proposals.after: Zhuge Liang and Fa Zheng differed in temperament yet esteemed each other by public duty.
proposals.reason: 公義 is public righteousness/duty, not office; 相取 is mutual regard grounded in that duty.

proposals.before: Once Liu Bei took the throne he aimed east at Sun Quan to wipe away Guan Yu’s defeat—counselors pleaded in vain.
proposals.after: Once Liu Bei took the throne he aimed east at Sun Quan to wipe away Guan Yu’s shame—counselors pleaded in vain.
proposals.reason: 恥 means shame/disgrace, not specifically defeat.

decisions.after: I believed Sun Quan’s defenses were directed northward and that he would need me as an ally, so I decided to go without hesitation.
decisions.reason: The Chinese remains in Liu Bei’s first-person speech. The existing narrative tag breaks the quotation grammatically; this revision restores the speaker and renders 所防在北 as defenses directed northward.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 孤以仲謀所防在北，當賴孤為援，故決意不疑。

decisions.reason: 許文休 identifies the second man by the courtesy name Wenxiu; it does not describe a younger man also named Xu Shao. The proposed wording follows the exact name form in the source without inventing a personal name.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 許子將褒貶不平，以拔樊子昭而抑許文休。

decisions.reason: 臣仲尼 makes Confucius Duke Ai’s minister; the existing literal translation reverses that relationship.

decisions.after: 〈The Chronicles of Huayang records that Du was from Guanghan and served as a provincial attendant.〉
decisions.reason: 華陽國志 is the work conventionally titled Chronicles of Huayang. The existing 'Records of Huayang Country' mistakes 國志 for an ordinary phrase rather than part of the title.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 《華陽國志》曰：度，廣漢人，為州從事。

decisions.reason: 孫夫人 is the title Lady Sun; 'Sun Lady' reverses normal English title order.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 近則懼孫夫人生變於肘腋之下

decisions.after: Even if someone else had advised him, as Emperor Wu of Wei believed, would that make him any less capable?
decisions.reason: The sentence continues the defense of rulers who act on good advice. It asks rhetorically whether receiving counsel diminishes Liu Bei; the existing wording instead invents a comment about Cao Cao’s vanity.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 魏武以為人所教，亦豈劣哉！

decisions.after: Those were merely bitter words born of wounded pride, not a fair assessment of the facts.〉
decisions.reason: The Chinese characterizes the preceding remark as residual language of shame and resentment and contrasts it with a measured judgment of reality. This revision preserves that logic without inserting named agents.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 此蓋恥恨之餘辭，非測實之當言也。

decisions.after: His son Miao was granted the rank of Marquis Within the Passes and rose to become Colonel of the Chariots and Administrator of Hanyang.
decisions.reason: 賜 means that Miao received a new grant, not that he inherited Fa Zheng’s posthumous title. The revision also renders 太守 consistently as Administrator.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 賜子邈爵關內侯，官至奉車都尉、漢陽太守。

decisions.after: Though Zhuge Liang and Fa Zheng differed in their tastes and values, they respected each other’s commitment to the public good.
decisions.reason: 公義 denotes public righteousness or the public good, not an office. The revision gives 相取 its reciprocal sense in natural English.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 諸葛亮與正，雖好尚不同，以公義相取。

decisions.after: Once Liu Bei took the throne, he prepared to march east against Sun Quan and avenge the humiliation of Guan Yu’s defeat; his ministers repeatedly remonstrated, but he ignored them all.
decisions.reason: 復關羽之恥 means to avenge the shame associated with Guan Yu’s defeat. The revision retains that concrete context while restoring the explicit force of 群臣多諫，一不從.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 將東征孫權以復關羽之恥，群臣多諫，一不從。

claimRetractions.reason: The name is an artifact of the mistranslation. The source gives Xu Jing’s courtesy name Wenxiu and does not name a younger Xu Shao.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 以拔樊子昭而抑許文休
